extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and policymakers interested in culture, religion, and national institutions (Victorian-era intellectual audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying normative criteria about 'culture' and its relation to religion, education, and political machinery as argued in a Victorian social-critique essay. The page sets standards for what counts as genuine culture, institutional aims, and how to judge reforms and church arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture as disinterested endeavour after man's perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture is 'the disinterestedness which culture... teaches us' and the 'disinterested endeavour after man's perfection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture should act independently of personal likings or political partisanship and choose means solely by whether they advance human perfection. It rejects actions driven by mere preference or factional interest and insists on impartial judgment toward the aim of total perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality — cultivation of the whole man
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture is concerned with 'the harmonious perfection of our whole being' and what Arnold calls 'totality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions and education should develop many sides of a person (intellectual, moral, aesthetic, spiritual), not merely a single practical or religious aspect. A true conception of culture serves the higher spiritual life by promoting many-sided cultivation rather than narrow vocational training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and flexibility regarding machinery/institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture shows 'flexibility' and 'independence of machinery' — it is not wedded to any particular institutional form (established church, free churches, types of statecraft) for achieving its ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture may approve establishments or free churches as instruments when they serve totality, but it will not cling to any machinery; it insists on the inward working toward perfection rather than on institutional forms per se. Examples: perfection can be reached with free churches as with established ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact with the main current of national life
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishments 'tend to give us a sense of a historical life of the human spirit' and place individuals/institutions 'in contact with the main current of human life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being connected to broad, public institutions (e.g., major churches, universities) supplies cultural nourishment, historical perspective, and opportunities to cultivate new sympathies; isolation in 'hole-and-corner' groups tends to stunt totality and cultural growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities and higher instruction must promote 'sweetness and light', not mere vocational training
rubrics_metrics.description: A university should cultivate 'sweetness and light' and total culture, not be 'calculated to produce miners, or engineers, or architects, not sweetness and light' (critique of purely practical training exemplified by Ezra Cornell's university).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher education that focuses only on practical knowledge produces intellectual mediocrity; genuine cultural education requires serious higher instruction that cultivates general intelligence and refined moral/aesthetic sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Hebraising provincialism — do not let narrow religious zeal exclude other spiritual sides
rubrics_metrics.description: Hebraising (the narrow, predominantly religious activation of the spiritual side) 'keeps [people] from culture and totality' and produces a 'narrow conception of man's spiritual range.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the religious side alone is awakened in a narrow way, it swallows other spiritual sides and causes provincialism. Cultural development must guard against such one-sidedness in religion and social reform (e.g., revivalist tendencies, sectarian fervour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain Hebraism's devout energy while balancing it with Hellenism
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Hebraism can produce provincialism, it supplies 'devout energy' and an intense discipline of faith that culture should value and sometimes restore; culture must balance Hellenising breadth with Hebraic earnestness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture should not discard the productive moral energy and discipline taught by Hebraism (e.g., the emphasis on 'doing' and faithful earnestness); instead, it must integrate that energy within a broader pursuit of totality so that zeal is informed by breadth and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and regularize popular church-discipline to integrate Nonconformists
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal that a 'Presbyterian or Congregational Church... be established... side by side with the Episcopal Church' to unite Protestants and check 'endless splitting into hole-and-corner churches.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and institutionalize the substantial, non-essential forms of church government (popular authority of elders) so that Nonconformists are brought into contact with national life; such accommodation can promote cultural totality among broader populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject Mialism — avoid doctrines that divorce groups from the national life
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept 'Mialism; that is, of a doctrine which leaves the Nonconformists in holes and corners, out of contact with the main current of national life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies or doctrines that aim to place all individuals in a formal equality by cutting off the connecting institutions risk isolating groups and undermining cultural growth. Remedy should focus on reintegration rather than universal detachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be pliant about non-fatal matters; fierce about truly fatal delusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture 'is all the more disposed to be pliant and easy about what is not fatal' but has a 'keen sense of what is really fatal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize cultural opposition to delusions that truly endanger totality (e.g., mistaking machinery for inward progress or mistaking bathos for the sublime) while tolerating minor or non-fatal differences in institutional arrangements or opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge reforms by inward working and spiritual effect, not by mere machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture insists on the inward working toward perfection and warns against mistaking 'machinery' (political reforms, institutions) for the real work of culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political and social reforms by whether they produce genuine enlargement of mind and character (inward effect), not merely by their procedural or institutional form (e.g., extension of suffrage, abolition of church-rates, or abolition of the Irish Church may be proper or not depending on their spirit, not only their form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake natural taste for the bathos for a relish for the sublime — exercise critical discernment
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture 'insists that men should not mistake, as they are prone to mistake, their natural taste for the bathos for a relish for the sublime.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining cultivated taste and critical judgment is essential: one must guard against superficial or popular enthusiasms being presented (or believed) as profound cultural achievement. Culture's role is corrective and educative in matters of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance popular education with serious higher instruction to avoid intellectual mediocrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries that 'have created an enseignement populaire considerable without instruction supérieure sérieuse' will 'expieront longtemps encore leur faute par leur médiocrité intellectuelle' (popular education without serious higher instruction leads to intellectual mediocrity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational policy should pair broad primary education with strong higher education and advanced instruction so national intelligence and general culture do not remain superficial and coarse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of men of culture: inward working, not seizing power
rubrics_metrics.description: The author 'does not wish to see men of culture asking to be entrusted with power' and suggests their proper address is: 'Know thyself!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those committed to culture should focus on inward cultivation, critique, and education rather than seeking political office; their contribution is shaping minds and tastes rather than exercising power directly.
